newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ post-election market volatility seen as limited.
newsitem.headline: NZ post-election market volatility seen as limited.

text.p: New Zealand's general election on Saturday has left financial markets in suspense over who will form the next government, but economists expect volatility to be limited when markets re-open on Monday.
The country's historic first election under a proportional voting system offered little fresh information to trade on, they said on Sunday.
A spokesman for ratings agency Standard and Poor's (S&P) told Reuters the election result was "not terribly surprising" and that S&P was broadly comfortable with it.
Results were very much in line with pre-election opinion polls, and show a clear victory for neither the right nor the left.

The incumbent National Party's potential coalition partners failed to attract the support needed to assure its return to power. National won 44 seats in a 120-seat parliament, gleaning an extra nine seats from supportive smaller parties on the right.

To form a majority government, the main opposition Labour party, which won 37 seats, would need the support of the left-wing Alliance (13) and the economic nationalist New Zealand First (17), if not in formal coalitions then at least on matters of confidence.
The balance of power lies with Winston Peters' New Zealand First party, which wants to cut immigration and limit foreign stakes in "strategic" assets to less than 25 percent.

Peters has refused to say who his party favours as a coalition partner. Both National and Labour say they will be negotiating with Peters, but economists believe New Zealand First is more likely to jump to the left.

Bancorp Treasury Services executive director Roger Kerr said Peters would take his time in to decide who he would support and markets would grow increasingly nervous the longer it took to resolve the make-up of the new government.

"Markets like certainty, and this is going to be a fairly drawn out affair...I don't think the markets will go into a fury on Monday, but as things progress and it looks like it's going to be drawn out, they'll start to reflect that uncertainty.
"How much it will cause a sell-off in bonds and the Kiwi dollar remains to be seen," Kerr told Reuters.
He said there was always the chance New Zealand First Party would not enter any formal coalition.

"If he (Winston) does just hold out and does nothing, and allows (Prime Minister Jim) Bolger to form a minority government, that's reasonably positive for the markets and would be good for interest rates. But I think the higher probability is that he goes with Labour," Kerr said.

ANZ chief economist Paul Stewart told Reuters he would be surprised if the currency weakened substantially on Monday. Continued buying interest from exporters, combined with ongoing dual currency bond issues, would limit its weakness.
Labour proposes to take a more flexible approach controlling inflation by widening the current zero to two percent targeted band.
ASB Bank economist Anthony Byett said markets would take comfort from the far left Alliance Party's poor showing.

The fear had always been that the Alliance, which campaigned on promises of free health and education, would have a strong representation. "That hasn't eventuated, so that's one fear you can cross off the list," Byett told Reuters.
